I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. On August 12 the under secretary of state, in accordance with an order of this house, tabled the total election expenses on behalf of each candidate by constituency in the general election of March 31, 1958. With regard to the constituency of Winnipeg North Centre, which I represent, my total election expenses were shown in the amount of $10,680. Subsequent to the tabling of this information in the house a Canadian Press report appeared in many of the newspapers in this country carrying this information, and in particular it was published in the Winnipeg Tribune on Thursday, August 14, under the headline "$10,680 to defeat Knowles".
This figure is totally incorrect. My official agent informs me that in accordance with section 63 of the Canada Elections Act he filed a summary of the return of election expenses on behalf of myself with the returning officer for Winnipeg North Centre, which summary of election expenses was published in accordance with subsection 5 of section 63 of the Canada Elections Act, and which shows the total amount of my election expenses for the March 31 general election to be in the amount of $5,409.42. We do not like certain aspects of this bill, Mr. Speaker. It is for this reason I propose to move an amendment to third reading. We realize that today some countries, notably the United States, appear to have surpluses as we do in Canada. We have noted that the western world has gone through similar situations in years gone by. We consistently have in mind the years beginning with 1928, 1929 and all the 1930's. We note that at that time the wealthier, more self-sufficient countries of the world such as the United States and Canada thought the answer to their problem was to raise and to continue raising tariff walls, thereby hoping to provide employment within the borders of their own countries.

Mr. Speaker, we saw how disastrous at that time that policy was. We saw that higher tariffs led to retaliation and to a limitation of world trade. We feel that for the solution to our economic difficulties and in order to provide full employment in Canada we need more and not less international trade. This bill in certain aspects calls for the raising of tariff walls. We feel that the Canadian people at this time should definitely turn their backs on the old and discredited remedy of tariffs. It is for that purpose that I now move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch):
That Bill No. C-50 be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole with instruction that they reconsider tariff item 554b of part IV of schedule A.
That particular part of the act which we feel should be reconsidered by the committee of the whole, or that particular section, calls for a higher tariff on imports of wool into Canada. We feel that the expressions of opinion the Conservative party gave to the Canadian people at election time, namely that it was in favour of increased trade with the commonwealth, could best be exemplified by lowering tariffs on goods coming to us from the United Kingdom. We feel that this is a reversal of the policy enunciated by the Conservative party in raising tariffs against imports from our best customer for many of our important products. We feel that raising tariff on any imports from the United Kingdom at this time will do a great deal of harm to the negotiations that are supposed to take place in Canada this fall-next month, I believe-among the commonwealth nations.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to speak at any length with respect to this amendment. It deals with only one item of the many in the tariff schedule. Our position was very clearly stated in previous stages of the debate. We had a division in the house on this matter at one of the earlier stages. This group is in favour of the amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Mr. Speaker, this subject has already been discussed on several occasions, and I am sure there is no reason now for an extended debate upon it. I simply rise to deal very briefly with the assertions made by the mover of this amendment, which continue to misrepresent the nature of Bill No. C-50 which is now presented to the house for third reading.
He has said that this bill represents a policy of high tariffs. That statement has no foundation, and to make it is to misrepresent the facts. The house has already been given the facts on several occasions during the course of this session, first on June 17 in the

budget speech, next when the resolution upon which the present bill is founded was before the committee of ways and means, and again in the earlier stages of the bill itself. The fact is that with respect to numerous items of the tariff, those with respect to zinc and zinc products, iron and steel and pipes and tubes, what is submitted to the house is a series of items many of which involve increases and many of which involve decreases in the existing tariff rates.
What has been submitted to the house in that respect represents the results of studies conducted by the tariff board on references directed to it by the former administration and recommendations which have the effect of reviewing items which have been in the tariff for many years, some of which have not been reviewed or studied for something like 30 years and which were badly in need of modernization. In the result, the tariff board has made recommendations which modernize the tariff and which rewrite sections and consolidate other sections. Therefore to say that the result of these items now submitted to the house is a return to high tariffs is to misrepresent the facts.
In the second place, this is pictured by the mover of this amendment as a policy of opposition to extended world trade, which is also a misrepresentation of the facts. This government has indicated its deep concern over the enlargement of world trade, and the policies which have been followed by the government and which have been offered to the house have been policies designed to increase Canada's trade. Canada's export trade has in fact increased since this government came to office.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to say anything on this matter, but the speech made by the minister which deals with so many important matters not relevant to this particular amendment makes it necessary for me to say a few words on the amendment. If I attempted to discuss generally the action the government has taken on tariffs I would, of course, be out of order as the Minister of Finance was out of order.
I will merely refer to page 1247 of Hansard, when in his own budget speech, mentioning the iron and steel duties which are very important elements in the tariff structure, the minister himself said:
A major result of these changes will be to make more effective the protection which it affords to Canadian producers.
Those words speak for themselves.
The minister said that as far as this particular item is concerned it will not prejudice in any way the forthcoming economic conference. I do not know how the minister can tell us that; I do not know on what evidence he can base a statement of that kind in connection with a conference which has not yet taken place and whose agenda we do not know. But if he has taken that position it is diametrically opposed to that taken by the wool exporters of the United Kingdom who, I submit, should be the best judges of their own interest and the best spokesmen with regard to the influence of this action on the forthcoming conference. I have already cited evidence to show that they have strongly objected to this increase in the wool duty and are worried about the effect it will have on the forthcoming conference. If the minister is not worried, they are.
We have opposed this item because it will not do anything effective, as the minister himself has admitted, to help the wool industry of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not true.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It possibly will give them a fighting chance. I believe those are the words used. That is all. But while it is not designed to give the wool industry an assurance of a profitable life in this country, it is designed to create indignation and uncertainty in the United Kingdom on the eve of this conference.
It is also an item designed to increase the duties against British woollens but not to touch the duties on woollens from countries, apart from the United Kingdom, whose exports of this product to this country are increasing.
As I have said before, Mr. Speaker, this item will not accomplish any good purpose. It will do some harm; it will do little if any

good, and for that reason we have opposed it in previous discussions of the subject, and also for that reason, as my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River has pointed out, we will support this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, any move by any government generally to increase trade barriers is one that should be opposed. Without question, in spite of the comments of the Minister of Finance, the fact remains that this is a serious increase in tariffs against woollen goods coming to Canada from commonwealth countries.
In taking part in any debate in this house the minister seems to use words which are not very often used by many members in the house, particularly when he himself is short of any real substance for his arguments. He says the speeches that have been delivered, or the speech that was delivered by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam was based on false premises, was a misrepresentation of the facts and so on. It would have been much more in keeping with sound argument for the minister to have dealt with this particular item itself.
This is an increase in the barriers against British woollen goods coming to Canada; this is a return to the policy of former Tory governments of increasing tariffs generally. This move is ill-timed; and for the minister to say that it is without foundation to contend that it will have a damaging effect on the commonwealth conference is to show that the minister has not followed the reaction in the United Kingdom, which was a very strong and very definite reaction against what Canada was doing. It expressed keen disappointment and concern that this would make positive results from the forthcoming economic conference more and more difficult.
While there has not been the kind of progress that we would like to see toward removal of trade barriers over the years, nevertheless since the end of the war there has been a very gradual whittling down of tariff barriers. That has gone on until the present action of this government, and we now see that trend being reversed. We see it being reversed in a very disturbing manner as far as this item is concerned. This is not a general increase in tariffs against every country in the world; it is an anticommonwealth move. This is a move directed against the United Kingdom; and it ill-be-hooves the Conservative party of all parties, I would suggest, to make any such change in tariffs.
This is the true line of the Conservative party; it is the historic line. It means that the Conservative party is reverting to its
Customs Tariff
historic policies and its historic role. But I would suggest that the majority of members of the Conservative party in this house, as well as the members on the opposition side of the house, did not campaign on a policy to increase tariffs, much less to increase tariffs against British goods. I express the hope at this time, Mr. Speaker, that we shall have some independence amongst the Conservative members; that we shall see evidence indicating that at least a few members, perhaps just a handful but at least a handful, will stand up and vote in the interest of lower trade barriers and against a move to increase trade barriers.
If there was one major thing that happened to the Liberal party to bring about its defeat it was the general practice that no matter what the government did, no matter how bad any move the government might make might be, their members always supported the government; there was no independent voice or independent action in their ranks. I express the hope this morning that in the ranks of the Conservative party we shall see some votes in the interest of freer trade and against this return to Tory protection.

That is why we favour the bill in its present form; in our opinion, section 41 should be adopted in its present form.
Let our hon. friends opposite have no fear; before long, I am fully convinced that the province of Quebec, like all the others, will take advantage of this bill. Besides is it not urgent that we adopt the bill as is? Indeed, it is not only the matter of donation from husband to wife that is involved. There is the donation of the farm from father to son, a time-honoured practice in the province of Quebec, whereby the head of the family, while still in good health, bequeaths the ancestral farm to his son.
In my opinion, delaying the passing of this provision would mean that tomorrow, in most farm homes of the province of Quebec, heads of families and their sons could not take advantage of a measure for which we are indebted today to the present government and for which I also wish to commend and thank the government.

Mr. Speaker, I have followed with a great deal of interest the points made by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Dorion).
I must say to him, at the outset, that we are by no means opposing the legislation in so far as it provides for an exemption in regard to the setting up of the son on the family acres. Indeed, we all recognize that this measure brought forward at this time by the government is extremely sound and we are all for it.
Now, when the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Dorion) enphasized that parliament had no right to amend the Quebec civil code, we share his views and the federal government cannot legislate in the matter. However, until the situation was clarified, the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) wanted to submit that payment made by a husband to his wife under their marriage contract when the husband wants his wife to benefit, be considered as a gift. That is what the hon. member for Hull meant.
Will the hon. member allow me to ask him a question?
Yes.

Does the hon. member know that any donation under a marriage contract may be sometimes considered as a gift in case of death? It all depends on the way the gift is made. Precisely because of the complicated phraseology of a marriage contract, could not the house possibly find some solution in this matter?

I shall answer my hon.
friend right away. I recognize that, in the province of Quebec, a sale or gift between husband and wife is prohibited. But there are exceptions. When, for instance, the husband makes a matrimonial gift to, or confers some benefit upon his wife under the contract, he has the right to draw up a written instrument explaining his motive. There is also the case when the husband pays his wife for reserved assets; if he lists in the contract the reasons for the sale, he is entitled to do so. Those are the three exceptions included in the act and confirmed by jurisprudence.
There ought to have been some amendment under which section 41 would provide that, in the province of Quebec, any gift to the wife in payment of matrimonial advantages or of reserved assets, be exempt.
We all know very well that the federal government has no jurisdiction as far as amendments to the civil code of Quebec are concerned. Along with my hon. friends I feel that the Quebec civil code has ensured
57071-3-242
Income Tax Act
the survival of the province of Quebec. We are proud of that body of legislation which protects the citizens of our province.
What the hon. member for Hull had in mind was that clause 41 should have been amended to ensure that payments made by a husband to his wife under the terms of a marriage contract, as well as whatever is owed in respect of reserved property, be considered as gifts for the purposes of this act.
(Text):

Mr. Speaker, there is actually no fine line of demarcation between the two points of view expressed, but I would like to address myself to the point raised by the hon. member for Bellechasse, whose legal opinions I, and all those who live in the province of Quebec, have come to respect. He is perfectly right when he says this is a matter which could be remedied by the legislature of the province of Quebec; that is perfectly clear. There is however, one clear fact, a brutal fact if you like, and that is that we are enacting legislation which does create a prejudice, a prejudice which might be remedied but which might not be remedied. That is the point we are making.
We realize that only the province of Quebec can amend the civil code and rectify what I consider to be and what I have argued is a prejudice. Whether the legislature of Quebec will or will not amend the civil code is something which is not known to us. It is quite possible that the debate which has taken place in this house may draw the attention of the Quebec legislature to this issue and may, as a consequence, provide the remedy. If we had not raised this question it may not have been drawn to the attention of that legislature, which is the authority which can bring about a change in the code. I feel, as a member coming from the province of Quebec, that it was our duty to raise this issue. It is perfectly true that in principle we approve legislation to make possible gifts of this nature, but we felt that unless this step was taken to encourage the finding of a remedy, then a prejudice might remain.
I feel that the hon. members from the province of Quebec have done their duty in raising the issue, and in so doing they have laid their fingers on a prejudice now being created by legislation of the parliament of Canada. That is all we did. Whether a remedy will be found we do not know, but I repeat it was our duty to bring this matter to the attention of the house. I still think if the Minister of Finance had accepted the suggestion which was made, namely that he should address himself to the Supreme Court

Finance-Special Warrants of Canada or to the Department of Justice in order to endeavour to obtain their support of his opinion, then we might have been convinced. He has failed to do this, and we feel that prejudice has been caused, a prejudice which might or might not be remedied.
I appreciate the argument made by the hon. member for Bellechasse, and I hope that perhaps with the help of his colleagues on the other side of the house the matter may be drawn to the attention of the legislative assembly of Quebec in order that the prejudice which the parliament of Canada is now causing to the people of Quebec may be remedied.
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.

I do wish to point out, however, that in the short time in which I have been able to look over the document I have not found much to support the claim which has been made during previous appropriation bills this session, and particularly on December 6, when the Minister of Finance gave the impression that certain reductions along lines which would involve economies and eliminations of extravagance and so on were involved.

I think such an interpretation might be placed upon the minister's remarks last night. He made reference to the fact that certain reductions had been effected in the amounts originally contained in the book of estimates for 1957, and pointed out that $1,270,000 were reductions made in committee of supply last session and that $112,795,000 were reductions effected by order in council.
I just want to indicate to the committee that we cannot anticipate that these reductions are giving effect to economies. I have looked over this document very quickly, as I say, in the short time available to me, with attention to some of the items indicated as involving reductions, and I think every member of this committee will realize that most of these items represent merely deferment of expenditures and that no cancellation or elimination is proposed.
For example, item 797 is one of the largest items. It refers to a reduction of $10 million in respect to wheat and flour being provided to India and Pakistan. I think the committee will realize that there is no cancellation involved here; there is simply a deferment, and the expenditure will occur in a subsequent year. There are other items where the reduction concerns statutory obligations.
I think of item 465; 668 which refers to maritime freight rates, a subsidy given to the railways. If the railways carry a certain quota of freight they are given this public subsidy, and a reduction is claimed there of $1,200,000. Hon. members will realize that this reduction took place simply because the traffic on the railroad was less than was anticipated. Had the traffic equalled the original forecast the amount mentioned in the item would have been expended.
Another item, 197, involves $4,500,000 with respect to our contribution to the provinces in connection with vocational training. I do not think the minister or anyone else would claim there would not have been a desire to make this expenditure if certain provinces had taken advantage of the legislation we have enacted, or that we would not have been happy to have made this expenditure for this purpose.
The big item, is, of course, item 240, a reduction of $32 million with respect to defence. I hope that during the committee stage after second reading of the bill either the Minister of Finance or the Minister of National Defence will at long last give us the details with respect to the items in the large "basket" item which accounts for this claimed reduction. This information was sought when the defence expenditures were considered in part on December 5, but we have not yet been able to get the details

connected with this very large item. I hope we will be able to get a breakdown during the committee stage.
Then we find another large item here, $9 million with respect to the St. Lawrence seaway. This is item 532. I think hon. members will realize that this does not represent the elimination of any expenditure; it is simply a deferment, and when construction proceeds in a subsequent year the item will be picked up. I am not sure what the situation is with respect to item 525, a $7 million reduction with respect to capital advances to the atomic energy commission, but I assume that here again the situation is the same; that construction did not proceed as quickly as was anticipated in the fiscal year and that the amount will be spent in a subsequent fiscal year.
Let us take another large item, $10 million with respect to the Colombo plan. This is item No. 872. I think all members of the committee will remember that there was some pride taken in the fact that there was to be an increase in the amount to be spent in connection with the Colombo plan work, and I ask the minister if it is not a fact that if this $10 million was not spent in the last fiscal year, cheques will be issued in the current fiscal year which will pick up this item of $10 million.
As I say, I have looked at this matter hurriedly, but this appears to be the situation. The minister said on December 6 that certain reductions were taking place, but that none would be in the field of construction or would affect employment. However, when we see the details here we find that a very substantial amount which had been appropriated for the construction of airports was not in fact spent. We find that there was an underexpenditure of some $3 million in public works. The Minister of Public Works is here and he may be able to tell us whether or not this involves deferment or whether these represent cancelled items. In any event they are construction items.
Then we have another item of $2,200,000 with respect to the Veterans Land Act. Again, no one will think for a moment that there was any cancellation of our standing offer to veterans who wish to acquire property. This simply means that toward the end of the year it was realized that applications were not being approved in the number that was anticipated at the beginning of the year, and there was an underspending of $2.2 million. I do not believe the government would really want to have that particular saving.
I think they would have been pleased if satisfactory applications had been received in such numbers that this particular item could have been spent, which would have assisted our veterans.

I think one realizes fully that owing to the changing conditions under which we are living today, and the great expansion that is taking place in this country, problems arise suddenly which are not foreseen when parliament is sitting. In this respect I wish to bring to the minister's attention a news item which I noticed in the London Times this morning, dated August 19, which 1 think, indicates that other governments as well as ours are having problems because of changed circumstances and conditions in modern society. I want to read it and ask for the minister's opinion on the suggestion contained in this news item. It reads as follows:
The appointment of a small independent committee to report on the theory and practice of treasury control of expenditure is recommended by the select committee on estimates in their sixth report.
The committee, bearing in mind the handicaps they met in a limited examination of treasury control over expenditures, say that the proposed committee should have access to cabinet papers.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman. As hon. members are aware, my department was before the standing committee on mines, forests and waters a few weeks ago. Members of that committee were given the opportunity of reviewing all aspects of my department, including particularly the 1958-59 estimates.
The report of the standing committee has now been made available to all members of the house. It is pleasant for me to note in the report that the committee feels that my department is doing a good job, but the committee also feels that more should be done in order that the "normal national development be not delayed".
With this recommendation in mind I do feel that the minor increase requested for my department for the present fiscal year will meet with the full approval of all members of the house.
I should now like to review for the house the main activities of the five branches of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, namely the surveys and mapping branch, the geological survey of Canada, the mines branch, the dominion observatories and the geographical branch. The department also has a mineral resources division which is concerned with all matters of an economic nature pertaining to the development, utilization and conservation of Canada's mineral resources. In addition, the department administers the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act and the Explosives Act.
The department continues to experience a heavy demand for base maps for resources development, defence, transportation, engineering and such purposes. Moreover, the department must meet the growing need for research and investigational work into the development of new scientific tools and new methods to assist industry in the search for and development of our mineral resources.
For some time my department has been handicapped in coping with the increased demand for its services by cramped quarters in scattered parts of the city. A few years ago a building program was started to provide the modern facilities necessary to carry out efficiently the department's primary function
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys of assisting Canada's mineral industry to grow and develop. This program is progressing favourably and is expected to be completed late in 1961.
To enable the department to continue to carry out its function of assisting resources development we are asking for $29,742,151. This is exclusive of the dominion coal board estimates, and represents an increase of $1,762,761 over the previous year's estimates.
The main items accounting for this increase are: (1) salaries and wages, reflecting the general increase in salary and wage rates; (2) the cost of buildings and land, some of which is now reflected in the estimates of each department rather than in the public works estimates; and (3) the cost of scientific equipment required for expanded programs and the additional laboratory space which we shall have in our new buildings on Booth street. I shall explain the other increases over the previous year's estimates as I proceed.
The department, through its surveys and mapping branch, carries out the two functions of establishing a network of surveys over the length and breadth of Canada, including the Arctic islands, and of providing base maps for use in the development of Canada's natural resources.
The surveys and mapping branch is divided into five divisions, the geodetic survey of Canada, the topographical survey, the Canadian hydrographic service, the legal surveys and aeronautical charts division, and the map compilation and reproduction division. In addition, the Canadian section of the international boundary commission reports for administrative purposes through the branch director.
This year the house will be asked to vote the sum of $8,743,130 to provide for the continuation of the branch's mapping and charting program. This represents an increase of $363,184 which I shall account for in my remarks on the appropriations for each division of this branch.
The geodetic survey provides the original surveys that form the framework or basic control for mapping throughout Canada, and for engineering and surveying projects related to natural resources development. We are asking for $690,761 for the survey's 195859 program, an increase of $113,503 over last year. This increase is due mainly to the higher cost of air transport as the survey extends its operations farther northward.
The topographical survey is responsible for the medium and large scale mapping of Canada. It has a twofold objective, to complete the mapping of the whole of Canada at the scale of 1 to 250,000, and to provide topographical maps at the scale of 1 to 50,000,
3826	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys or approximately one inch to the mile, for areas which are of immediate or potential importance in resources or other development.
For the topographical survey we are asking $1,929,769, an increase of $107,895 over last year. This is mainly accounted for by higher operating costs in more northerly areas.
The Canadian hydrographic service charts Canada's coastal and inland waters. It operates, this year ten ships, seven on the Atlantic coast and three on the Pacific, and seven shore-based parties using large launches equipped with echo sounders.
A number of recent developments have made it necessary for the service to extend its charting program considerably. The construction of the St. Lawrence seaway, for instance, has resulted in a demand for up to date charts of the St. Lawrence-great lakes waterway. The exploration and development of mineral deposits in northern areas, particularly in Ungava and the Northwest Territories, have made it necessary to chart adjacent waters to provide safe ore-shipping routes. The potential development of Canada's Arctic regions, the entry of Newfoundland into confederation, and the withdrawal of admiralty charts of Canada's Atlantic and Pacific coast all mean expanded charting operations to meet the need for charts of these areas.
Though the program of work is on the increase, there are certain non-recurring items, and the amount of $3,898,092 required in this year's estimates represents a slight increase only over the previous year.
The legal surveys and aeronautical charts division carries out original and subdivision surveys in Yukon and the Northwest Territories and in Indian reserves, national parks and other federally controlled lands. It also produces electoral maps, aeronautical charts, and the Canada Air Pilot the last two of which are used by airplane pilots over Canada. The appropriation for this division is $754,674, an increase of $49,867 over last year, reflecting the general increase in salary and wage rates and increased travelling expenses for field parties.
This division also works with provincial agencies through appointed commissions in the demarcation of boundaries. This year work is being continued on the British Co-lumbia-Yukon-Northwest Territories boundary, on the Manitoba-Northwest Territories boundary, and on the Saskatchewan-Northwest Territories boundary.
The map compilation and reproduction division compiles, drafts, and reproduces maps and charts, and has charge of map distribution. The division's main problem is to keep its map publication abreast of the greatly


speeded up surveying, mapping and other field operations. For this fiscal year we are asking for $1,261,432, an over-all increase of $24,171.
There is a separate vote in my department's estimates to take care of all aerial photography needed by the several departments of our government. The main use for this aerial photography is necessarily for topographic mapping. We have practically completed the coverage of the Canadian mainland by vertical aerial photography and because of the growing importance of the far north in the scheme of things today, we are starting this year to expand this aerial photographic coverage into the Arctic archipelago. For the coming fiscal year the department is asking for an appropriation of $1,050,000 to cover the photography of the archipelago.
We turn now to the geological survey of Canada. It studies, maps, interprets and reports on the geology of Canada. The geological survey's work is needed to make known areas of potential sources of minerals and to assess the nation's mineral potential. The activities of the branch are based primarily on field investigations. The survey supplements these investigations by essential and specialized research in all phases of the geological sciences including geophysics, geochemistry and mineralogy.
For the fiscal year the geological survey requires an estimated $3,114,720, an increase of $444,854 over last year. Part of this increase covers a moderate expansion in the survey's field program for 1958. It is placing 77 parties in the field this year compared with 69 last year. The increase also covers an expansion in its airborne magnetometer and reconnaissance surveys, and in its laboratory facilities for research. Such facilities are vital to a scientific organization such as the geological survey.
Now that the branch hopes to occupy its new quarters and laboratories on Booth street next year, the estimated expansion of laboratory and related equipment is much greater than in recent years. An appropriation to cover this new equipment is required during the current fiscal year so the full potential of the new quarters may be realized as soon as possible.
The geological survey is giving top priority, first, to completing the preliminary reconnaissance mapping of Canada at the earliest practicable date and second to the development of more rapid, economical and efficient field techniques.
To this end the survey turned to aerial reconnaissance by helicopter in 1952. Since then it has carried out seven major helicopter projects in which it has mapped nearly half

a million square miles of territory. In general the helicopter technique has proved to be the most economical in terms of dollars per square mile. This year the geological survey will carry out the second part of the helicopter operation which it began last year in northwestern Quebec in a 120,000 square mile area lying between James bay and Hudson bay and the Labrador trough. This is the largest unmapped portion of the Canadian shield.
The survey has resumed airborne magnetometer work in the maritime provinces this year to complete the unfinished sections of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. It is also making an aero-magnetic survey of the continental shelf in the bay of Fundy, Northumberland strait, and the gulf of St. Lawrence to gain information on the geological features of the shelf.
Our mines branch has several projects in hand. Its chief function is to promote the economic development and conservation of Canada's mineral resources by means of metallurgical, chemical and mechanical research. The mines branch is divided into five divisions; mineral dressing and process metallurgy, radioactive minerals, industrial minerals, fuels, and physical metallurgy. We are asking for an appropriation of $3,536,390 for the mines branch for the fiscal year. The increase of $158,609 over last year reflects the continued expansion in branch activities to keep pace with the expansion in our mineral industry.

Canada's present front rank position as a major world producer of uranium is a direct result of much painstaking work and research

Now that most uranium companies in Canada are in production, the division is turning its attention to the recovery of other values from radioactive ores, and to the improvement of present recovery processes.
The industrial minerals division is concerned with the economic development, treatment and utilization of Canada's resources of nonmetallic minerals, sands, clays, rocks, and industrial waters. These make up, in large part, the raw materials of the chemical and construction industries.
Canada's output of these minerals has expanded greatly in the past ten years along with our country's rapid industrial growth, and the wide variety of projects under way in the division's laboratories indicates the importance of these minerals to our country's continued industrial growth. In a recent project, for instance, branch engineers did valuable work on methods of upgrading poor quality sand and gravel and processing crushed stone to make new sources of these much needed materials available for the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway and power project.
The main goal of the research and investigative work of the fuels division is the economic utilization of Canada's fuel resources. It is working, for example, on improving the quality and making saleable products of the low-grade oils and bitumen of high sulphur content which occur in large quantities in western Canada. To assist the coal industry it is working on the development of methods to reduce the hazards of mining at increasing depths, and on the development of cleaning and beneficiation methods to improve coal products and reduce wastage. It is also doing research on the blending of coals to provide high-quality cokes for foundry and blast furnace use.
The physical metallurgy division assists the Canadian mining and metal industries, the defence services, and the atomic energy project by carrying out fundamental and applied research on metals and alloys. It investigates the causes of failure of metal parts. It does applied research on the production of new alloys and the improvement of existing alloys, and fundamental research to explore some of the laws governing the behaviour of metals. It does much of its work in co-operation with industry.
At the dominion observatories, the course of world scientific events has greatly increased the work in astronomy and geophysics. The observatory's major participation in the international geophysical year, for instance, has
3828	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys meant a greatly increased program of observations and measurements of geophysical phenomena. It has also meant the establishment of two new magnetic observatories, one in Victoria, British Columbia, and one in Yellowknife, Northwest Territories.
For the dominion observatories we are asking for an appropriation of $1,769,036, an increase of $833,872 over the previous year. Of this increase $562,750 is to be used to permit the branch to expand its astronomical research to include radio astronomy. It will cover the purchase of a radio telescope, the acquisition of land, and the construction of buildings and works for the establishment of a complete radio observatory this year near Penticton, British Columbia. Radio astronomy has proved to be the most spectacular development in astronomy in the past 20 years. When completed, the new telescope will be one of the largest radio telescopes in North America. We expect to have it in operation in 1959.
The increase in the observatories appropriation also includes the purchase of a new 48-inch telescope by the dominion astro-physical observatory at Victoria, British Columbia. The building to house the new telescope is expected to be finished during the present year, but the telescope itself will take two more years to complete. The addition of the 48-inch telescope will permit the observatory to make fuller use of its 73-inch telescope for long-term programs of observations.
Our geographical branch carries out surveys of various parts of Canada, and collects and organizes geographical data on Canada and on foreign areas of importance to Canada. The work of the branch will be similar in scope this year to that of 1957-58. The appropriation is estimated at $315,728 for the fiscal year, an increase of $21,685 over last year, mainly because of the increasing remoteness of field operations. A major project of our geographical branch is the making of land-use surveys and terrain-analysis studies. Such land-use mapping is proving particularly valuable in southern Canada for purposes of planning and development. The special Senate committee on land use visited the branch in November, 1957 to learn about this work.
The preparation of the atlas of Canada by the branch has been under way for a number of years, and I am pleased to inform the house that the publication of the English edition is scheduled definitely for December of this year and possibly earlier, and that the French edition should follow next year. The atlas illustrates the broad range and great wealth of Canada's known natural resources-
[Mr. Comtois.l

agricultural, forest, mineral, fishery and water-a wealth from which we in this country produced a gross national product valued at over $31 billion last year.
The atlas, however, does not illustrate the vast potential of our resources still to be discovered or developed. Nowhere in Canada is this potential greater than in the mineral industry. The evergrowing richness of our country's mineral potential is most evident in the continued discovery of tremendous reserves of iron ore, particularly in Quebec; of base metal wealth in the various provinces; of oil and gas in western Canada; while in the territories, exploratory activity and the large scale reconnaissance mapping being carried out by our geological survey are steadily confirming the same rich potential in these great northern regions. In view of this, there can be little doubt that our mineral industry will long continue to contribute a major share to our national prosperity.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, I should like to pay a tribute to the very excellent and efficient service being rendered by the employees of my department. They are making a valuable contribution to the impressive growth of our mineral industry.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
The first item in the estimates of this department gives the members of this committee an opportunity to review the activities of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. We also have a chance to comment on the industry most directly concerned with the department.
I was very much interested in the statement made by the minister this morning. It is true, as he said, that the estimates of his department have been studied by the standing committee on mines, forests and waters and many of the hon. members in this chamber had an opportunity on that committee not only to question the minister but also to question the officers and the directors of each branch of the department. The minister, of course, made a lengthy statement in committee regarding his department, which was very much appreciated by all the members in attendance. At the same time we had the opportunity to review the activities of the dominion coal board and there were lengthy discussions on that subject.
I noticed that this morning the minister did not say anything about the dominion

coal board, but I presume that in view of the fact that this board practically constitutes a department of its own, of course under the minister, that he will let us have a separate statement later on with respect to the activities of the dominion coal board.
With respect to the work of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, we all realize that the tremendous expansion which has taken place during the last 20 years in the development of our natural resources, and the intensity of the mining activities in practically every part of this country has of course caused an extraordinary large demand for geological information in the form of reports and mapping services, research work and tests on Canadian ores and minerals and other services provided by the five principal branches of the department, so much so that the ability to supply the necessary information has been taxed to the maximum.
We are often inclined to think that the department is not keeping abreast of the developments which have taken place. However, those who are engaged in the search for new mineral deposits, those who are directly engaged in the installation of new mining developments and those who are trying to improve mining operations and extractive methods in mines, have only praise and compliments for our federal department and this is due in great measure to the efficiency of the personnel of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. I have said before and I would now like to repeat that we are most fortunate in having excellent mining engineers, scientists and other experts who are highly qualified, each in his own sphere. I wish to congratulate them upon the work they have done and I am sure that if this department is voted the necessary funds to permit an increase in personnel and an expansion in the activities of the department, hon. members can rest assured that the net result will justify such an increase in moneys voted by this house.
Some very important work has been carried out by the department and we have only to read the annual reports which are published to see the excellent work which has been done in the past. I repeat that it is unfortunate that, as members of this committee, we do not receive the report on past activities before we consider the estimates for the coming year. The department at one time published a summary report which was most helpful because we received it soon enough so that we might consider it before the estimates came before the committee. This method of procedure has been dropped and I understand that the annual report is not now ready in time for us to consider it in this way-and this applies to the reports of other 57071-3-243
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys departments of government. However, we have been told in committee that next year efforts will be made to produce such a report before we are asked to study the estimate and I hope that if it is not possible for the queen's printer to produce the normal annual report we will receive at least a preliminary report as we did in the past.
Regarding the different branches of the department, I will have quite a few questions to ask the minister as we proceed to discuss the estimates but at this moment I would like to extend my remarks to the mining industry in general.
We are aware at the present time that the situation in the Canadian mining industry is not as we would like it to be. We have, however, every reason to be optimistic and to believe that in the long term it will fulfil its great promise. In recent years the industry has played an outstanding role in the development of the Canadian economy and at the present time it is a very vital factor in our economy; its future is almost unlimited. The general softening in the price of base metals on world markets during the last 16 to 18 months has been reflected in the Canadian mining industry. The demand for most mineral products has diminished and of course prices have dropped. This trend was much accentuated in respect of copper, lead and zinc, but fortunately the price of copper tends to increase at the present time. The prices of the two other metals are, however, extremely low.
For instance, the price of lead and zinc dropped by approximately 20 per cent and 25 per cent respectively, during the period 1956 and 1957 and, of course, the price of copper had declined by 40 per cent until lately when we saw a small rise in price. In Canada these adverse conditions in the prices of copper, lead and zinc have had serious repercussions. Several mines have suspended or closed their operations, and others have cut back production. The outlook for the mining industry in the immediate future is not too good. The three major base metals, copper, lead and zinc, are experiencing some serious trouble. Copper stocks in the United States are not very high at the present time, but there is an incentive by way of a bill which has been passed, or which will be passed, to enable the government of the United States to pay subsidies not only to copper producers but to producers of lead, zinc and other metals. This will certainly produce an effect in this country; though I am told it may not be as severe as the tariffs which were supposed to be imposed on these different metals being exported to the United States.
3830	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
Nevertheless, I think the future of the mining industry is bright. It may take some time before the price of metals goes up again, but we know that consumption will increase. Often we are asked by people who are not familiar with the metal trade why we believe consumption will increase. The increasing use of minerals is partly the result of a growing world population, partly the result of wartime demands and partly because of the improvement in the per capita wealth of the population. By and large, people are better off today than ever they were, and generally speaking the higher the standard of living the more metal is used. In addition, if we look through the different reports which are published we will soon realize that the consumption of metal will be increasing in the future to a very large degree.
First of all, we have the opportunity to read the Paley report which was published in the United States, and this report stated in part that from 1950 to 1975 the overall demands for minerals would probably be 90 per cent higher in the latter year despite the fact that today in only two metals, magnesium and molybdenum, is the United States self sufficient. The reserves have been depleted and they are actually importing large quantities of these metals, and in the near future this importation of foreign metal into the United States will be increasing all the time.
By 1975, the report states, the increased needs in the United States will be greater by the following amounts. Then the report goes on to give a table of the estimated increases. The figures have been public for quite a long time, but they do show the great opportunity which our minerals industry has to supply an important part of the metals which will be imported by the United States in the future. Here is a partial list: ferro-alloys, 75 per cent, nickel 100 per cent, tungsten 150 per cent, cobalt 344 per cent, manganese 50 per cent, molybdenum 170 per cent, copper 43 per cent, lead 53 per cent, zinc 39 per cent, titanium and cadmium 324 per cent.
Canada has many of these metals in exportable quantities, and production has been on the increase. In the case of some of the others there has been a sharp deficiency. However, I see by reading the report on the economic prospect prepared by the Gordon Commission that the following appears on page 215:
The basic influences which have operated to increase Canadian mining and mineral processing production in the past will in all probability continue to be felt with undiminished force in the future. The population and standards of living of all of the main industrial countries of the world

are continuing to rise, with expenditures on durable goods tending everywhere to increase even more rapidly. Defence requirements may decline relatively from their present level, but competition and technological change will combine to put heavy emphasis on investment in machinery and equipment, while the economic development of the less industrialized countries will add still further to the demand for minerals. One must, of course, make allowance for the increased absolute amount of scrap metal which will be available-
This has always been a factor. However, on reading these reports we must realize that the future of the base metal industry in this country is very bright.
This brings me to the activities of the department itself. I have always stated, when I have had a chance to speak on occasions such as this during the discussions of the estimates of the department, that we in this country should make more money available to the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. I know it was mentioned by the minister this morning that the estimates for this year amount to $29,545,451, while in
1957-	58 they were $27,979,390. In other words, there has been a very small increase. But the minister said this morning that this increase is mostly brought about by increases in salaries and wages and in the extra cost of building. I understand that building costs were probably carried by some other department in the past but are now being carried in the estimates of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. The minister also stated that increased cost was involved in the purchase of scientific instruments and other installations. Thus, even if the estimate for
1958-	59 does show an increase of over $1 million as compared with the estimates of 1957-58 the increase is not such as to permit an extension in the research, mapping, geological surveys and other works which is supposed to be done by this department. If you look at the estimates for 1956-57 and 1955-56 you can see that they have been practically the same for the last four fiscal years; there has been a small increase, but that increase has not been sufficient to permit the department to do the job that it was designed to do or to give an opportunity to its officers and staff to do the job they would like to do.
I do not want to repeat myself, but we have experts in this department. They are able to do a job, but the department has to be voted the money necessary to do the job. I will go so far as to say that the minister is anxious to do a good job in his department. Since he has taken over the department he has shown that he is very much interested. Every member of the House of Commons should insist that the estimates of this department be increased. We have a job to do.

Let me cite only one example. We were told in committee that only about 30 per cent of this country has been mapped for geological purposes. We were told that last year we added 3 per cent to that. That makes 33 per cent, which means that we still have a big job to do. I realize that from now on the work will probably proceed more quickly. We are using methods today which are facilitating this work. For instance, in 1952, in the geological surveys of this country, we initiated a program of helicopter operations. In the magazine Precambrian, largely prepared by officers of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, there appears a report of the operations. Because the report has been prepared by those officers I think we can quote it without question. In 1952 we had one helicopter operation. This was the first one. It was called the Keewatin. In 1954 we had three operations, the Baker operation, the Pitt lake operation and the northern Cape Breton operation; in 1955, we had two; in 1956, we had one; and in 1957, we had two. I understood from what the minister said before recess today that we have another operation in Quebec this year which is called the Fort George operation. It started in 1957, but we were told in committee that the department expects to complete this operation this year. I understand also that next year the department contemplates the possibility of having other operations such as those I have mentioned. In the same article in the magazine to which I referred there is a report on an operation called Mackenzie. These helicopter operations are really the thing. Probably we can do more work in these operations than we could do with the usual method of making geological surveys across the country.
In saying that the department has completed only 33 per cent of the program of mapping this country in so far as geology is concerned, I am not trying to belittle the work of the department. They have done good work. We have to remember that 25 or 30 years ago those who were making the surveys had to travel by canoe and they could not do very much in one season because it is easy to understand that this work cannot be carried out during the winter. We should try to do more geological survey work. This is very important. I was told not very long ago by some mining people that the reason why the federal department of mines should do more work is that their work is tops, their work is first-class and is of great help to prospectors when they go looking for new metal discoveries. They say that they get more information from the federal department of mines than they can get from the different provincial departments of mines.
57071-3-243J
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
We had a good example of that in one instance in Quebec last year. In Quebec we have a section over which a geographical survey was carried out by a private company a few years ago. Since 1949 I have insisted that the work which was done by that company should be compiled and published. Finally, in 1954 or 1955, we succeeded in having the department start compiling those maps. When the maps came out a year or two years ago the first map which gave information regarding the survey in that part of Quebec was compiled by the department of mines in Ottawa, and the department was given permission to publish the information. After a certain number of years those maps were published. What happened? Immediately after they were distributed prospectors used them and mining companies used them and the result is that in the province of Quebec we have about the biggest discovery which has been made in the last 25, 30 or 50 years. Ninety miles north of Senneterre they discovered a deposit of zinc, lead, copper, silver and gold, and we have there what looks like the biggest deposit discovered in this country up to now. They have proven over 30 million tons of ore and I am sure the work which will continue will double this amount. I may be optimistic, but it looks like a big mine for the future.
Those who are not familiar with the situation may say, "We do not need lead and zinc right now; we have an over-supply of those metals". Mr. Chairman, the time will soon come when we shall be glad to mine this deposit of which I have spoken, and we shall soon be glad to open up Pine Point in the Northwest Territories and develop those other big Canadian mining prospects.
To show how important is the work of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, the total estimates of this department, as I mentioned before, are close to $30 million. I will agree it is a substantial amount, but when you compare those estimates with the estimates of other departments and when you take into consideration the great need for exploration across this large country of ours you realize that those estimates could very well be doubled and they would not be too large.
I have spoken only about the geological survey branch. I could say the same things about the survey and mapping branch and about the mines branch. They are all important branches of the department. Given the proper amount of money those sections of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys could double their work. It was mentioned by the minister in the committee that it was difficult at times to organize parties to make surveys during the summer
3832	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys and early fall because of not having a sufficient number of leaders for such parties. I suggest to the department that they should secure a greater number of surveyors and geologists and train these men. If the department does not train such men, how can we expect the department to have a sufficient number of leaders to take charge of these parties during the summer seasons? It is very important that we try to enlist in the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys a sufficient number of technicians and experts so that when we want to carry out a certain amount of work, whether surveying or geological surveying, we will be able to do it.
I have just one word in conclusion. I know my time has almost elapsed. I congratulate the officers and personnel of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys but I should like to go a little further and congratulate a man who is ready to retire from one of the branches of the department. I am thinking of the director of the surveys and mapping branch. This man has done a lot for the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys and in so doing has done a lot for his country. Although I am sorry to see him leave the department because he has to retire I am also proud that he will be replaced by a man who has lived in my constituency. Sometimes we are disappointed to see a man go but are proud of the man who fills the vacancy and in this case I am very proud that the man who will replace the director of surveys and mapping is a man who has lived for some time in the constituency of Villeneuve. I will have questions to put when we come to the individual items and I will also have something to say about the dominion coal board after the minister has made a statement.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister's disarming smile plus the technical nature of the work undertaken by the department are not components likely to engender political turbulence in the chamber this afternoon so I trust that we are going to have a very good natured, objective discussion of the minister's estimates.
I must say that I read with some interest the proceedings of the committee that considered the estimates of the department and I noticed that the good work of the department and the staff was recognized by the committee as I think it is recognized generally. A good many Canadians do not realize the excellence of the personnel of this technical department, of the men who are willing to serve Canada in their present positions when in a number of cases they


could obtain higher salaries in private industry and possibly very much higher salaries if they left Canada and went to the country to the south of us. I think that fact should be recognized more by Canadians generally.
The second conclusion I draw from reading the proceedings of the committee, having in mind the good work being done by the department and the excellence of the staff, is that there is a necessity for more funds to expand the good work being done and give this excellent staff the opportunity to do things that are waiting to be done in the technical field in which they work. I believe it is correct to say that this department has rendered service to the country for 51 years. I do not intend to make extended remarks at this time because I have to leave to record a radio broadcast and I must not disappoint the many people who listen to me every week as the fount of all wisdom with respect to what is happening in parliament.
However, the surveys and mapping branch, in which I have been particularly interested, is of great importance to the country at this time especially in view of the development of our natural resources, water resources, forest resources and so on. I have three suggestions to make to the minister. The first is that I hope every possible opportunity is given to students from universities and technical schools to secure employment with the field parties of this branch during the summer months. I also hope that every opportunity is given to graduates to secure positions within the department.
With respect to students particularly, the experience gained in field work is of great value and I think it is very worth while to get these young men started as undergraduates and interested in the work of the department, which means so much to the country. I hope every consideration is given to that because I have had representations from a number of organizations urging that, especially in the light of present circumstances, every effort be made by the government and particularly this department to find employment for as many of these persons as can be fitted into the appropriations voted by parliament.
My second suggestion has to do with the markers that are placed by the branch in various parts of the country and which are of great value in determining levels, locations and things of that sort. They are usually bronze plates with a number and possibly some reference to the fact that they are the property of the government of Canada. They are of great interest to many people and I suggest to the minister that consideration be

given to placing a little more information on these markers. They are placed there as the result of considerable expense involving surveys, levels and things of that sort, and in addition to having the reference number and the fact that the marker was established by the government of Canada I think it would be advisable to consider putting more information on them relating them to the surveys of the district, their purposes and so on. I make the suggestion because of the number of people who are interested in these things and the marker, of course, means nothing to them until they write for the information related to the number on the monument.
My third suggestion is that the branch is in need of more publicity. Field parties go into a district and the local residents know there is a field party there because some people are living in a few tents by the side of a lake who go to the nearest store and buy a few groceries. They know there is somebody there working for the government of Canada and doing something. I think the opportunity is being lost to acquaint our young people with the value of the work and its purpose and I suggest that there should be more publicity generally, possibly by press releases to the local papers, informing the people of the district that there is a party from this branch of the department doing survey work in the district. I also think that, using the right personnel, local organizations and school children could be informed of what is going on through short talks. I am sure that could be worked into the department's agenda without any great inconvenience. I suggest that it would be of great advantage to the local people and particularly the younger people from the point of view of getting them interested in the surveys and their purpose and helping them to realize in that way the value of the natural resources in their own district and developments in Canada generally. I think we should do everything possible to spread knowledge about the purpose of the work of the branch in its relation to the development of our natural resources.
I want to say a few words about the Canadian board of geographical names, an organization in which I have always been interested. In that connection, I want to ask the minister if there is close liaison between the officers of his department and the corresponding branches of the provincial governments with respect to the accuracy of names or the inclusion of names on maps. In recent years I have noticed two or three instances where a recent provincial map, say of the province of British Columbia, contained names that
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys you could not find on a map published by the Dominion of Canada. I was just wondering if there were any continuing relationships to make certain that these changes in names or these additional names are included in the latest map produced by this department.
With respect to the Canadian board on geographical names, I want to deal particularly with one matter on behalf of a good number of the pioneer residents of the district which I have the honour to represent. I should like to express their appreciation to the minister for certain action on his part in recognizing the good work of Dr. L. E. Borden, who was on the cruise of the Neptune in 1903 as medical officer and botanist. In that connection, I am going to put two letters on the record because I have been asked to do this by persons interested in this question. The first letter is dated Ottawa, February 12, 1958, and reads:
Mr. G. M. Munroe, Secretary,
Canadian Board on Geographical Names, Department of Mines and Technical Surveys,
No. 8 Temporary Building,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Munroe:
I would like to draw your attention to the name of Dr. L. E. Borden after whom it has been suggested a physical feature in the Kootenay be named.
Doctor Borden has been a resident of the Kootenay for over 50 years and has made considerable contribution to Arctic exploration.
Doctor Borden's record was brought to the attention of the house on the estimates of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys on July 5, 1956 (Hansard 5692-95) -
That was the occasion on which I brought to the attention of the house his good work on the cruise of the Neptune.
-and later presented the proclamation to the house on August 11, 1956 (Hansard 7433).
That was when I presented this, as far as is known, only existing copy of the proclamation whereby the Arctic islands were taken possession of in the name of Canada.
May this request be investigated at your earliest convenience and a report forwarded to me accordingly.
Yours sincerely,
(sgd.) Paul Comtois
I am very glad to read that letter into the record. I am more than pleased, as a good number of the people in our district are, over a later letter written by the minister. It reads:
Ottawa, June 26, 1958.
Mr. T. Eric Jones,
2998 Seaview Road,
Ten Mile Point,
Victoria, B.C.
Dear Mr. Jones:
I wish to refer to our exchange of correspondence regarding the naming of a geographical feature after Dr. L. E. Borden.
3834	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
The Canadian board on geographical names has notified that the U.S. board of geographic names
now advised me that approval has been given to apply the name of Borden river to a feature which flows into Roes Welcome sound between Cape Fullerton and Whale Point to commemorate Dr. Borden.
The feature is in the area visited by the Neptune and is identified on the enclosed map for your convenience.
Yours sincerely,
(sgd.) Paul Comtois
I want to thank the minister on behalf of the many friends of Dr. Borden who was a pioneer resident of our district, was a medical officer of the 54th Kootenay battalion in which I had the honour to serve as did the Minister of Public Works, was the Conservative member of the legislature for a number of years representing the Nelson district, and during all these years since his return after the cruise of the Neptune has rendered great service to his district.
