subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
The minister was well
informed of the circumstances. I am one of those who believe in pioneers being recognized in the naming of these geographical features. Some years ago I was horrified to find, after a certain crew had returned from surveying a certain area in western Canada, that they were so lacking in names that they had named the various points, things such as lakes, rivers and physical features, after the camp cook and so on. I am not objecting to these people getting places named after them, but these places should not be named after someone who comes from eastern Canada to spend six weeks in the area. I am all in favour of those pioneers who wandered into the woods having their names commemorated in the naming of these geographical features. I may say that is C.C.F. policy, Mr. Chairman. In any event, I know the minister's action in this respect is appreciated by a good many pioneer citizens in the Kootenay district, in fact in British Columbia, because they believe the good work of Dr. L. E. Borden should be recognized.
I have one other matter I should like to mention under this heading of the Canadian board on geographical names. I asked the minister a question this morning about this press report which is headed "Ottawa Puzzled as U.S. Names Seaway Lake". I was very pleased with the minister's reply so far as the action of Canada was concerned. The report, you see, reads in part as follows:
Although Canada has taken no official action- and did not seem aware today that the United States had-the Canadian board of geographical names is expected to follow the U.S. lead at a meeting-in early September.
Residents on the U.S. side of the lake behind the giant international powerhouse have been

approved the name Lake St. Lawrence July 24.
-Officials of the Canadian geographical board said today they had been in contact with their U.S. opposite numbers regarding the naming of the lake but did not know that the United States had already acted.
Now, my point is this: I am somewhat mollified by the fact that Canada suggested the name lake St. Lawrence. I do think it is somewhat discourteous of the geographical board of the United States to make this announcement instead of waiting until there could be agreement so that there would be a joint announcement made by both countries. I am sure that all members of this house realize that is the proper way to do things. If you extend the courtesy to another country, then you expect proper procedure and protocol. That is all I am going to say because the minister's explanation this morning gave me some comfort. I can go and tell people that, as a matter of fact, we named it and they announced it.
I want to say a few words generally with respect to the administration of the Explosives Act. I do not usually deal with explosive matters, but this is a serious matter because of the peculiar circumstances that have existed in the Kootenay district for a number of years. I have discussed this with the Minister of Justice and with other officials, and I have discussed it with the local people in my constituency. We feel there are good reasons why there should be a rather more rigid administration of the Explosives Act by the minister's officials. In that connection, I want to read briefly from a letter from a man who travels a lot around the district. He writes me as follows:
I would like to point out that there has been no proper control over the handling of blasting powder and dynamite, and regulations are very lax in the direction and use of powder by most of the large companies in this area. As you will have noticed recently in the paper, a case of blasting powder was found in the near proximity of slashing for the gas line and I suppose you have also heard of powder being left loose along the side of roadways on government projects.
I have had occasion to investigate and found that most of the logging companies could not tell me how much powder was used on a particular project and there have been no actual checks by any authority of the amount of powder used. This resolution is to attempt to get a stricter enforcement of all such use of powder and proper inspection at all times to prevent further misuse of same.
I would like to point out also that there is nothing to prevent me from going to the C.I.L. and buying blasting powder without too much restriction. Further to this, I feel that when the gas line was put through the Nelson area there was no proper control as to who was handling the powder all during this project and a lot of powder could actually have been stolen, even a stick at a time.

Then in addition to that, I have a resolution from the Nelson-Trail and district labour council. This resolution was adopted at a general meeting of the council after prolonged and detailed discussion of this problem as it related to the Kootenay district in general. The resolution reads as follows:
Whereas,
The blasting of power poles, Canadian Pacific railroads and now with the bombing of bus transportation public waiting rooms and restaurants, causing much distress to our workers;
Therefore be it resolved that:
(1)	That blasting powder be charged as the responsibility of one man in any company, or others, and that he be held responsible for the distribution, checking and the correct reports and tallies of all such explosives being used.
(2)	The inspection of all such store houses- arsenals, powder houses where explosives shall be stored in the West Kootenay shall be inspected at least once a week.
(3)	The inspections-tallies-records of explosives, etc. shall be under the control of a federal government official.
Of course, in passing that resolution I suppose the members realized that the matter is in a theoretical sense under the control of the federal government officials. But you cannot expect the officials to be visiting all these places continuously. I suggest that under the circumstances there is need for a much stricter enforcement of the Explosives Act. I have gone through logging operations and have seen two or three cases of dynamite left by the men building roads, just under a log or something of that sort over the weekend. I have been on road building operations and over a weekend there would be left powder and dynamite just possibly covered up with canvas or put under a large machine or something of that sort. In addition to that, dynamite and powder can be purchased by farmers legally and properly through the local farmers' institute which buys it, I think, at a somewhat lower rate from the C.I.L.
I think the great majority of persons using powder are careful to store it and lock it up over the weekend and things of that sort. However, I myself have observed some slackness in this direction. In view of the particular circumstances I urge that the minister give some consideration to the matter. Our circumstances are somewhat unusual. I am not going into that matter now. The minister knows the circumstances. I suggest that he discuss the matter with the Minister of Justice and see whether, at least under present conditions, we could not have a somewhat stricter and, shall I say, abnormal supervision and administration of the Explosives Act in our district. That is all I am going to say in that respect. That is about the only suggestion with a tinge of complaint that I am going to make this afternoon.
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
I just want to say a word or two about the geological surveys which are of such great value in this country in the search for minerals. I should like to ask the minister, when he replies, whether he would tell us what parties will be operating or are operating in British Columbia this year and whether there are any parties of the geological surveys branch working in the southern interior of British Columbia. Again I suggest that there should be some publicity with respect to the work of the geological surveys branch. It is doing a most interesting and valuable work. I think there should be more publicity through the press and local organizations, and that there should be some opportunity for even our high school students to know what is happening with respect to this most important work which may have some considerable effect on the Canada they will inherit and have to administer in later years.
I should now like to say a word or two about the mines branch and it will be very brief indeed. I represent a constituency in which mining is an extremely important part of the economy. I simply want to say that the good work of this branch and the service it renders to private industry are recognized by all persons who are engaged in the mining industry in my constituency.
Before leaving that point, in view of the fact that the matter was raised by the hon. member who spoke previously-to whose speech I listened with great interest and who is a member who knows what he is talking about when he speaks on this question; and by the way, I am not suggesting that I do not-I want to deal for a moment with the question of the market for lead and zinc. The minister knows, as do his officials, that owing to the present price for lead and zinc a good number of small producers are having a very difficult time. On the orders of the day some time ago I asked the minister, or possibly it was his alter ego on that day- I am not quite sure which it was-whether he had any knowledge of the global plan that was to be handled by the government in each metal-producing country to control distribution and export of lead and zinc according to the market demand after taking into account the prescribed domestic production level.
This proposal was made in the United States by senators representing mining states. I do not know whether or not the minister has any further information on that matter but from the information I have received this suggestion offers some opportunity for international planning of the markets for lead and zinc and, shall I say, the division of those markets on a fair basis
3836	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys related to the normal productive capacity of the countries that would enter into what is called in this report a global plan. When the minister replies I should like him to inform the house whether his department has any information with respect to this plan.
My concluding topic-those words, of course, will bring a smile to everyone's face -has to do with a matter which comes under dominion observatories whose work everyone recognizes. I raised this matter previously. I mentioned it to the minister I think on one or two occasions. I think the last time I mentioned it I suggested that it be brought to the attention of the dominion-provincial conference as a matter that could be properly discussed there and one that should not create much difficulty in order to give effect to it. While I know, as do we all, that in peacetime the question of daylight saving time comes under provincial jurisdiction, I think we are somewhat silly in that respect. I suggest that we should work towards a national daylight saving time. If we are going to have daylight saving time, let us have it apply on a national basis. I again suggest to the minister that he bring this matter to the attention of the next dominion-provincial conference or of the provincial governments individually, whichever course he thinks to be more appropriate, in order to see whether something cannot be done to establish national daylight saving time as a result of agreement between the federal government and all the provinces.
I think we are absolutely silly to go on in this way and have various times established at various times with all the inconvenience involved. I think the suggestion is only common sense and will be to the great convenience of the Canadian people. Then, if we had that sort of arrangement, as to the timetables of the railroads, all we would have to do is to say generally that they are an hour later or an hour earlier across Canada. At the present time we have the railroads running on standard time, some buses running on daylight saving time and some buses on standard time. Then there is a difference between the daylight saving time in various provinces. I think we are causing ourselves a great deal of unnecessary inconvenience because we have not common sense enough to get together and work out a solution to overcome what appears to me, and to the members of the group which I represent, to be a totally unnecessary inconvenience which is causing us unnecessary difficulty in travelling and things of that sort and at the same time in some cases unnecessary expense. I urge the minister to give consideration to our representations in that respect. If he is successful in bringing this about


before his estimates come before the house at the next session of parliament we shall rise up once again and say his name is blessed.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
There are two matters which I should like to bring to the minister's attention. I hope the two hon. members who have just taken their seat will excuse me if I do not follow them in their remarks. I refer particularly to the speech made by my colleague the hon. member for Villeneuve who always speaks with such authority on matters affecting the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys.
I always listen with interest to the speeches made by my hon. friend the member for Kootenay West because he succeeds in making anything he has to say interesting. He did cover the waterfront pretty well, but I want to dwell upon one matter which he brought to the attention of the minister, which is the names announced by the minister for the new international lake now formed by the pool resulting from the power development in the international section of the St. Lawrence river. If I understand the situation correctly, the name that has been suggested by the geographical board on names and which has received the concurrence of a similar board in the United States, is that of St. Lawrence lake. Of course I would have no fault to find with that name as it is a name which has behind it a great deal of history. However, I do have a name to suggest to the minister which I think is more appropriate and which I believe, not only meets the historic aspirations of those who live in the area in which this work is taking place but which I believe also meets the national and international viewpoints with equal, if not more, suitability than the name chosen. Of course my submission to the minister is made with great deference, but it is made without hesitation. Although the name has been chosen, I know full well that on other occasions when a name of greater significance has been brought to the attention of the geographical board on names that board has not hesitated to reconsider and to change decisions already made.
The name I have to suggest is one to which I submit serious consideration should be given, because it would serve to preserve the historical associations of the area in which this development is taking place. As the house knows, some of the most important historical episodes in the history of our country relate to this section of the St. Lawrence river; the exploration of the west, the Indian wars under the French regime, the coming of the united empire loyalists, the war of 1812 and the development of the Canadian

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
canals. This particular development with which we are now concerned is perhaps not the final stage, and it seems to me that the name I am about to suggest is more in keeping with the facts surrounding the area than the name selected.
Before these developments took place there existed in this area what was known as the Long Sault rapids. Those rapids have disappeared, having been destroyed by the power works constructed by both Canada and the United States. To those who live alongside the international boundary line and to those who have ever lived in the area, the Long Sault rapids were a sight which can never be forgotten, not only because of their beauty but because of their galloping wildness. The rapids carried many ships, first bearing the early settlers, and then many inhabitants of our country from one end of Canada to the other. The name I suggest, therefore, is the name of Long Sault lake, and the reason I do so is that the lake is on the international boundary line and the rapids themselves were partly in Canada and partly in the United States. It therefore seems to me that it is a name which should appeal to the United States as well as to Canada.
Furthermore, there is an island which bears the name Long Sault which is entirely on the United States side of the boundary line and upon which some works in connection with the project have been constructed and which, until the development of the seaway, had been practically unknown. There were two communities on the Canadian side of the line which have entirely disappeared because of the flooding, namely Mille Roches and Moulinette. These communities have now been replaced by a new community which has arisen on the Canadian side of the line and which also bears the name Long Sault. It would strike me, therefore, that the name of lake Long Sault or Long Sault lake would carry with it not only local support with respect to the early history but would also be national and international in character. So far as I am personally concerned it has far more significance and appeal than the other name because we already have the gulf of St. Lawrence, river St. Lawrence and St. Lawrence county, which is just opposite the works now under construction on the United States side of the line, and which county is in the state of New York. We have on the other hand very little in the way of commemoration of the name of Long Sault in this country. I therefore ask the minister if he would not be good enough to bring this name, which I submit with deference, to the attention of the officers who form the geographical board on names so that they
might consider it and discuss it with their counterpart members in the United States geographical section who have decided upon the name St. Lawrence lake.
Were the minister to accede to my request I am prompted to say that the name would receive universal acclaim.
The next subject which I would like to discuss is one which I am sure the minister is aware, is of concern to me because I have brought this matter forward previously in the course of the discussions on his estimates. This is the fact, the strange fact, that the boundary line separating Ontario and Quebec on lake St. Francis has not yet been determined. After many, many years it seems an anomaly, as it were, that this boundary line should still be in suspense, and I will continue to bring it to the attention of the minister every time I have an opportunity to do so. I do not need to do this because I know the minister is sympathetic in respect of this problem. I also realize that the minister does not have direct jurisdiction over a matter of this kind, which must be determined by the two provinces concerned. On the other hand he has a very great interest in this question in that islands owned by the federal government lie in this area. A good deal of work is being done in the river in respect of the development of the St. Lawrence and it is not known whether the men are working in the province of Ontario or the province of Quebec. Lastly, from the tourist standpoint, a man who fishes, traps or shoots in the area never knows from one moment to the next whether he will be apprehended by the law officers of one or the other province. All these problems arise because it has not been determined where the boundary line lies.
It is an old problem and a vexatious problem, one which should have been determined a long time ago. I am one who sat on the other side of the house for a long time and perhaps I should take some responsibility with respect to this matter but, on the other hand, I must immediately add that I lost no opportunity to bring this very problem to the attention of the minister's predecessor.
Fortunately a survey has been made of the area, a survey which was agreed upon between the surveyor general of the province of Ontario and the surveyor general of the province of Quebec many years ago. Those two surveyors agreed upon a portion of the southern boundary of Ontario and Quebec. That which begins at Coteau and ends at a point 500 feet west of what is known as Cameron's island or Thompson's island in lake St. Francis. But beyond that to the west, for a distance of almost ten miles, in an area
3838	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys which is heavily inhabited on the Ontario side and which is certainly inhabited to a large extent by summer residents on the Quebec side, though possibly not as heavily, the boundary line has never been delineated, and it seems strange that in this day and age it should not be possible to find a solution.
I brought this question to the attention of the premier of the province of Quebec when I was the president of the St. Lawrence seaway authority, and I brought it to the attention of the premier of the province of Ontario and I was assured by both the gentlemen that it would be given their consideration. I know there are difficulties in the way. But the difficulties are small. They are that the islands lie, in the opinion of the province of Ontario, entirely within the confines of that province, while in the opinion of the province of Quebec, they lie entirely within the confines of Quebec. But the islands, it seems to me, are not of such importance that it could not be found possible to draw the line which separates Ontario from Quebec in this area.
The Ottawa Journal-unfortunately I do not have the date before me, but I have a copy of the article which, I believe, appeared in November of 1957-drew attention to the fact that this 10-mile boundary dispute should have been settled a long time ago, and it states that the present situation has proved very awkward for workers and contractors developing the lake St. Francis section of the St. Lawrence seaway and that it has been equally annoying for summer cottagers, anglers, hunters and trappers who have seen game wardens of both provinces converging on them with summonses at the ready.
I do not know whether the situation is as bad today as is suggested in that editorial but it is one which, it seems to me, should not be allowed to continue much longer. May I make a suggestion to the minister? I know he has very convincing powers. I know, too, that he is the kind of person who would not wish to be offensive in any way. May I suggest that he should first approach the premier of his province and that, perhaps, he might then have his officials communicate with the premier of Ontario in an endeavour to ascertain if the boundary line cannot be drawn. It would be a good thing for the federal government and it would be a good thing for the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. If a bill confirming an agreement between the two provinces were brought into this house I am sure it would receive the ready approval of parliament, because this is a good thing and a thing that should be done. I therefore appeal to the minister with regard to these [Mr. Chevrier.l

two points and, knowing him as I do, I am sure he will wish to give them earnest and sympathetic consideration.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words in view of the point which has been raised by the hon. member for Villeneuve concerning base metal discoveries to the north of Senneterre which happens to be in my riding. I do not wish to delay the passing of these estimates in any way, but I rise merely to say that I agree with the hon. member with regard to what he has said, and that I support the observations of the hon. member for Kootenay West regarding the geological surveys branch, which is doing a great job and whose work is of high value to the development of Canada's rich mineral resources.
I mentioned this discovery at Mattagami lake in the middle of my riding during my maiden speech here last May. I am glad to say that my constituents were most happy that I said a few words about it. The only reproach they made to me was that I mentioned at that time that the discovery would compare with that at Pine Point. They thought I should have said it was much bigger than Pine Point. The hon. member for Villeneuve has made that point clear. Not only one ore body has been discovered but, so far, it seems there may have been three base metal discoveries. I have also been informed recently by a reliable source that a gold discovery has also been made in that area. I agree with other hon. members who have spoken this afternoon that the work which has been done by the geological branch of the department of mines has been most significant in bringing about not only these discoveries but many others across Canada.
Before closing, I should like to make a suggestion to the minister concerning the distribution of geological maps and reports. In past years these maps and reports were distributed free to prospectors upon request. I understand that some people and, maybe some companies, abused this privilege and that as a result the prospectors and the companies are now being charged for any such reports and maps they may require. I should like to suggest that in order to encourage prospecting all over Canada at least one set of maps and reports should be made available every year to prospectors who intend to do some exploration work in a particular area.
Finally, may I congratulate the minister upon the help he has extended to the gold mining industry through the subsidy which we discussed a few days ago and also express our gratitude to the officials of his

department who, I believe, are doing a really good job. I hope they continue this good work because if we want to open up the north country we need more surveys and we need their help.

subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
I suppose it is partly to the credit of the minister that for the first time in many years his estimates went to the committee, and having read the committee report I realize they got through a considerable amount of questioning in relation to the department. I must apologize that some of the questions I am going to ask arise from the fact that I was not able to be on the committee at the time the estimates of the department were before it.
I want to make one key point at this time and to do it I should like to start with a quotation from the report which the minister read to the standing committee on mines, forests and waters. I think it is an important point because the evidence I want to present in a sense tends to contradict the minister's statement. On page 102 he said, referring to co-operation with provincial and private interests:
Nor is there any duplication of our work with that of the provincial government departments and agencies. A main reason for this is that our work and theirs though it may be in the same general field of endeavour, differs in nature and purpose. The work of the provinces stems from their responsibilities in administering resources development within their borders, whereas our work arises mostly from the need for research on the technological problems of the mining and metallurgical industries. Our officials and those of the provinces are in frequent consultation and the possibility of duplication of effort is reduced to a minimum.
I wonder whether the minister's attention has been drawn to a report which appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail on June 3. It is datelined from Edmonton and it is headed:
Co-operation Urged in Geological Survey
I would like to read part of this report because it is in contradiction of the statement made by the minister here, or at least I think it requires some further explanation on the part of the minister. It begins:
More rapid completion of Canada's geological map could be expected from a clear-cut arrangement between the federal and provincial survey agencies. Dr. H. C. Rickaby of the Ontario mines department said today.
Dr. Rickaby, in his presidential address to the geological section of the royal society of Canada, noted that less than one-third of Canada has been mapped, and even a smaller portion surveyed, on a scale adequate for mineral exploitation.
A statement of the aims and policy of both federal and provincial survey would serve to clarify their respective fields of responsibility, he said.
In Ontario, Dr. Rickaby said, the policy is to make geological work as practical as possible, with
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys commercial considerations uppermost as it attempts to aid in promoting the mining interests of the province.
If other provinces have about the same policy, Dr. Rickaby said, theoretically the field of broad fundamental geological studies-both field and laboratory-would be left largely to the federal government's geological survey of Canada.
"Adequate funds for fundamental research in all branches of geology and geophysics should thus be made available to them for this purpose", Dr. Rickaby said.
"However, because there is really no sharp dividing line between the scientific and the practical, it would be unwise to lay down specific regulations. Nevertheless, an understanding agreement will always be necessary between the different governmental surveys."
He goes on to talk about the work of the geological survey of Canada and the number of people employed and he said:
Although the number sounds impressive when viewed in the light of the amount of field work still to be done it seems regrettably small.
One large oil company and one base metal company operating in Canada employ 80 and 75 geologists, respectively, on a full-time basis, he said.
The federal survey attempts to spread its operation uniformly across Canada, but now is obliged to spend much of its effort on field work in the Yukon and Northwest Territories as the only government geological agency. In Newfoundland and British Columbia, the survey has special obligations under the terms of confederation.
Mr. Rickaby said that in some parts of Canada the private exploration and operating companies are gathering, collectively, more geological information than the government surveys.
"Much of this information is naturally not available to the public," he said, "but in any scheme of national planning for co-ordinated geological studies the place and contribution of the private companies should be taken into consideration."
It seems to me that the gist of these remarks raises very serious questions about the operations of the surveys branch, both in mapping and geology. I would also like the minister to note something that I raised on the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, namely the point raised by W. E. G. Brown, who is now with Spartan Air Services, who was a survey specialist with the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. His point was that he got out of the government service because of a lack of co-operation between the various agencies and the private interests. He went on in his statement before the Senate committee on land use to state that the whole survey problem in Canada is not being attacked-that is the way I interpret what he said-on a rational basis. We are far behind the Russians in our approach and there is overlapping, with no real coordination to prevent this and to direct us along the line.
These are not the kinds of criticisms that have great political weight in comparison, say, with a hassle over whether we have a Canadian economic outlook or not; but
3840	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys they are so fundamental and important that I think we need further statements and explanations than we have had. Then I would like to see the case prepared and presented to the house. It will take some time, but it will give us an excellent picture of how this co-ordina'tion is worked out and the planning stages of the future of how geological surveys and mapping surveys are going to move ahead and cover the entire problem, and how it relates to the number of employees that the department is planning to add. We would like to know about the workload upon those employees. I think this is one of the most important questions we face in all kinds of economic development in the country. If Dr. Rickaby's remarks, or Dr. Brown's remarks, have any substance at all, then there is an implicit criticism of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys.
I would like to tell the minister that later on I hope to ask him some questions in connection with what his mines section is doing with regard to safety work in connection with uranium slugs and that sort of material, and just what co-relation is being carried out with the Department of National Health and Welfare and with other groups making studies throughout this world on the whole question of the effect of radiation and how the department in its meteorological studies is working on this particular aspect.
I also intend to ask him some questions in relation to scholarships and grants. I appreciate receiving from the deputy minister recently a report on the national advisory committee on research into geological sciences, but this report does not give any indication of the number of applications for research grants. The committee on scholarships and grants concludes, after a review of all the inadequacies of support for both undergraduate and graduate work and for post graduates, with this paragraph:
The above sums on top of what will be the overburdened budgets of the universities raise a serious problem. Where is all this money to come from? If it is not found it will dangerously curtail the much-needed increase in key personnel required by the mineral industry.
At the back of this report we have some interesting statistics on the number of students and the number of degrees granted in various industries in relation to the subject fields of geology, mineralogy and metallurgy. The figures are very disappointing when you consider that only 124 degrees were granted in 1956. This raises the whole issue of the contribution the federal government, through this department, plans to make in this specific field, and whether it is planned to do anything, as the committee suggests, along the line of considering getting into the field


of undergraduate work, and how this department in relation to this particular problem is working with the other departments to assist the universities in some way.
Those of us who have anything to do with university affairs feel that the students in the sciences and in the engineering subjects have much better opportunities for scholarships on the graduate level than in the arts subjects, even though we may feel that it may only indicate that arts are not moving and the sciences and engineering fields are rolling. When we come to that particular phase I have a number of questions I want to raise on the statistics, the number of people applying for grants, the number of students affected and the plans of the department in this regard.
One of the other points we raised last year is the question in relation to the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act and the inspections that are carried out. Last year the minister asked us to provide him with specific cases so that he could work on them. I have been trying to get specific cases, but I have to repeat I am in the state I was last year. There is nothing more than the ordinary gossip you get from the miners going around the mining communities, but with all due respect to the miners they are not experts in terms of the ore values existing in these various mines. Therefore I should like a statement from the minister this afternoon as to how often his inspectors visit these mines and just what procedures they follow in order to determine that the mines are not low-grading their properties in order to take advantage of this assistance. If some publicity could be given to the techniques that are used and if it could be generally recognized that they are adequate and that there is no low-grading going on I think you would create a much better relationship between the managements of the mines and some of the people in the areas where the mines are being operated.
Another point I should like to touch on which has not been referred to is the whole question of the publications of the department in relation to popular usage. As the minister and his deputy minister no doubt are aware, prospecting is becoming more and more a big company proposition. It is very interesting to look at the summary contained in a reference paper put out by the Department of External Affairs entitled "Iron Ore in Canada, 1957". This was prepared by W. Keith Buck of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys and the indication throughout is that almost all discovery and exploration work is being carried on by very large organizations.

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
I think the minister must be aware that in most communities, especially in the Lau-rentian shield, there is a large number of what we might call small people who are anxious to get out and do better and more intensive prospecting. We have that situation in my riding. There is an active prospectors' association which is carrying on an adult education program. They are trying to improve their own standards. I have spent some time discussing with the members of the executive of this association what they might expect from the federal government in this regard. One of the main things they say is that the material available from the geological survey and the mines branch is excellent, as has been mentioned several times today, but how does the novitiate, let us say, in this particular field find out about it?
At the lakehead several large mining companies have their geological headquarters. Anyone who visits them will find that almost without exception they have practically a complete file of all geological survey and provincial mines branch material. They have it all arranged. They have men who know how to go into it. But the fact remains that the ordinary person operating with nothing more than the dominion government's annual catalogue or the consolidation issued by the department is not going to get very far in discovering what maps, memoires or reports he really wants to see.
I can give examples to the minister and deputy minister from my own area. There have been a number of reports on the Thunder bay region. The most valuable ones to the prospectors were those produced largely in the 1920's by a man by the name of Tanton. There was also a valuable reprint last year of the Thunder bay region which we appreciated. But there is no way that the ordinary prospector, not the big mining company, can go to the bulk of the geological survey material and find an adequate index. Why do you not have a consolidated listing of what you publish? Up to 1927 you had a very adequate index so that one can get right into old reports going back to the 1860's, but for all your most recent reports you do not have adequate indexing.
I know it is an expensive and difficult matter but if the department would do it in the same way as it did with its old indexes and as the provincial government used to do with the indexes to its bureau of mines reports you would open up much more information for the ordinary prospector than is available at the present time. As a matter of fact, I suggest to the minister that at the
present time the publications of his department, especially the geological surveys, are so complicated in the various forms in which they have been issued and the publicity on them is so hit and miss as far as the average person is concerned that it is really only the experts in the field who can take advantage of them. That is fine. We expect that perhaps the most fruitful results from these publications will come from the larger organizations but it seems to me that the department is not doing enough to bring its publications, especially those of the past, and all they contain to the average prospector or person interested in mining. Whether it is too expensive a job or whether it is even worth considering I do not know, but I should like to have a statement from the minister on how the department looks at the problem. I suggest to him that at the present time there is too large a gap between the ordinary person interested in mining and prospecting and the publications of the department.
As I am sure the minister and the deputy minister are aware, even the old geological survey and bureau of mines reports do not become completely outdated. There is always valuable information in them. I know this is true from the fact that so many prospectors have made use of geological survey files of which I have been in charge. They keep coming in and they are willing to go back to reports in the 1870's and 1880's in order to get the lay of the land and certain tips as to what these early geologists saw in the area. Possibly I have overemphasized the point but I wanted to put it as clearly as possible because I think there is room for the department to do more.
There is another point I want to mention. speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE EXPENDITURES AUTHORIZED BY SPECIAL WARRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, since the
early stages of confederation, the coal industry in Canada has always been a matter of concern to the government of the time, so much so that I sincerely feel it is free of any and all political interests. From time to time various bodies have been set up by both major parties to examine the Canadian coal situation and to establish policies on subsidies where and when needed. Many forecasts and outlines have been published and, for the benefit of some members, I have no hesitation in referring to the outline of the trade as presented by my predecessor in 1955 and recorded in Hansard on Monday, July 5 of that year, wherein the picture of the future was presented. Because of the increased interest in Canadian coal such bodies as mentioned above have invariably concluded that financial assistance should be provided by parliament to promote the movement of coal from the mines of eastern and western Canada to the markets of Ontario and Quebec, both as a measure of self-sufficiency and for a more equitable financial treatment.
After a period of trial and investigation as to cost, a policy was established whereby the government would assist towards the cost of transporting Canadian coal. This would permit the consumer in specific areas in central Canada to purchase coal at the same price as he would have to pay for imported coal. It should be noted however, that as these conditions changed so did the rates of assistance so that the widest area within reasonable limits could be provided with the Canadian product. However, in two cases, assistance has already been provided outside the areas of competition, but only where there was assurance of substantial business.
The Canadian product is not subsidized to sell for less than other coals, nor is it subsidized as against any other form of energy. The assistance granted only permits
the consumer in central Canada to choose between Canadian and imported coal at the same price level. It became apparent earlier this spring that the demand for coal during the year could be expected to decline because of continuing dieselization of railways, the increasing competition from other fuels, the comparatively mild winter and the increasing amount of secondary hydroelectric power from high water conditions, plus new hydro plants.
Faced with these conditions, the competitive area was widened, potential market areas received an increase of the maximum payments set out in orders, and the existing preference in favour of Canadian coal was doubled to 20 per cent where purchases by government departments were concerned. This resulted in a substantial expansion for Canadian coal in Ontario outlets.
In spite of this assistance, Canadian coal production in the first six months of this year was 714,000 tons or 11 per cent below that of last year, and imports of coal during the same period were down by 4,731,000 tons or 51 per cent, clearly showing a great reduction due to the causes noted earlier. The question, therefore, is how much more can be justifiably provided to benefit this one particular industry and to protect it fully against general changes in the national economy. In the case of Nova Scotia coal the maximum subvention provided is $5.25 per ton plus a further protection of 50 cents duty per ton on imported competitive coal or a total of $5.75 to move one ton to the present limit of the subvention area. In 1957, to provide one day's work per man meant the movement of 2.6 tons at a cost of $5.75 per ton or a total of $14.95. This is the present limit only, and further extension to provide more employment would mean a higher cost per day's work provided.
Turning to western Canada, the present maximum assistance is $4 per ton with the same duty of 50 cents on imported coal or $4.50 in total cost of assistance or again a cost of $18 per man for his output of four tons. To find any new outlet for western coal, would mean moving the coal to Ontario at a subvention of about $9 per ton or more, bringing the cost per man per day to $36. New outlets for reasonable tonnage are being investigated but this demands both time and care if the future trade is to be built up on a firm and lasting basis. Keeping the above in mind, the report of the royal commission on coal concluded that there must be some limit to the assistance provided and the subvention should be in relation to the cost of imported coal. Though we agree, it is the feeling of this government that present
[Mr. Herridge.l
conditions have justified assistance at rates somewhat higher than those contemplated by the commission.
Since Sir John A. Macdonald provided the first measure of assistance in 1879, the Conservative party and the Liberal party have both maintained and extended the policy of assistance to our Canadian mines, and I can safely affirm that this assistance to the basic industry is a measure that will receive our continuing support. The present picture is not a pretty one and the causes of the industry's deterioration are not easily set aside by any government action since they are the natural interaction of developing forces. Free competition could be replaced by a policy of control and dictation and there might be some improvement, but even then, who can guarantee that the prospective dictator would not use his authority to favour gas or oil?
I have tried to show that the subvention policy as applied by this government as well as by our predecessors, has been of assistance to the industry. The amount of money the committee is being asked to vote, however, may not be sufficient to maintain the present scale of assistance, since there have been changes in the economics of the industry in the last few months.
May I say that the administration of government assistance has been in the hands of the dominion coal board which has also the even more important duty of maintaining a constant study of the coal situation and of recommending to the government such measures as, in their opinion, would be of benefit to the industry. The administration vote presently before you is, I submit, a modest sum to pay for the services and work done by this board.

We had a report presented and read by the chairman-a very enlightening report-and we were able to question the officers of the department, because the board is considered as a department.
I wish at this time to congratulate the officers and the staff of the coal board for the excellent job they have done since the board was organized and, as the minister, stated I think the board has been very useful not only to the industry itself but to all those who depend on this industry.
